questions.q: What does the lesson's code-review table deliver that a vague 'looks good' review doesn't?
options: A specific, checkable account of which requirements from Lesson 21 are met and which aren't, line by line
A single overall pass/fail grade with no detail
An automated score generated without human review
A list of every line of code in the project
questions.explain: The review table checks each Lesson 21 requirement individually against what was actually built, producing a specific, checkable account rather than an unstructured impression -- directly mirroring the specificity Lesson 21 demanded of the requirements themselves.

questions.q: Why does the lesson treat the missing QAOA statevector check differently from the missing experiment records for reported results?
options: They are treated identically, since both are simply 'not done'

The statevector check is a genuine acknowledged gap needing future work, while experiment records aren't yet relevant because no experimental results have been reported yet -- only library code and test runs exist so far
Experiment records are more important so they get flagged as a bigger failure
Neither is a real issue and both can be ignored
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly distinguishes a genuine gap (QAOA statevector check, which should exist but doesn't) from something that isn't actually missing in context (experiment records, which Chapter 4 built specifically for reported experimental results -- and none exist yet to report).

questions.q: According to the lesson's whole-course checklist, what should be true of any result that is actually REPORTED (as opposed to just a library existing)?
options: It should never be documented to avoid cluttering the repo
It should have a git tag, a committed lockfile, and an experiment record with seeds/shots/backend version (Chapter 4's full reproducibility chain)
Nothing extra is needed beyond the code passing its tests
It only needs a screenshot
questions.explain: The checklist's Chapter 4 line specifically ties the full reproducibility chain (tag, lockfile, experiment record) to any REPORTED result -- distinguishing library code existing (no report yet) from an actual claimed experimental result (which does require the full chain).

questions.q: Why does the lesson say an explicitly documented known limitation is 'categorically different from, and far more trustworthy than, a silent gap a user discovers later'?
options: Because documentation length is the only measure of quality
Because silent gaps are always smaller in practice than documented ones
Because documented limitations make a project seem bigger
Because a user who's told upfront what hasn't been validated can make an informed decision, whereas a silently undocumented gap misleads them into trusting something that wasn't actually checked
questions.explain: This echoes Lesson 23's and Lesson 4's honesty principle: an explicit 'not yet validated' statement lets a user calibrate their trust accurately, while a silent, undocumented gap risks the user assuming broader validation than actually exists.

questions.q: Why did the capstone deliberately scope to only three small algorithms rather than attempting broader coverage, as stated back in Lesson 21 and reaffirmed in this closing lesson?
options: Because more algorithms were technically impossible to implement
Because the point was to actually practice the engineering disciplines (testing, architecture, reproducibility, estimation) end to end on a few algorithms, not to maximize algorithm count
Because the course ran out of time and had to cut scope unexpectedly
Because quantum algorithms cannot be tested in groups of more than three
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly reaffirms Lesson 21's framing: a small scope let the course prioritize actually exercising every engineering practice (testing tiers, backend abstraction, reproducibility, resource estimation) in depth, which is the actual skill being built, not algorithm-count breadth.
